summary.title: How to teach yourself hard things
summary.one_liner: Learning to learn is a set of practicable skills: pinpointing what you don't understand, becoming certain of what you do, asking good questions, and researching well.
takeaways: Turn vague confusion ("I don't get it") into specific, answerable questions; this is the most important learning skill.
Make knowledge you rely on fully certain (e.g. TCP ports are 16 bits, so max 65535) so you don't second-guess it while debugging.
Ask questions well: find the right communities (Slack, IRC, mailing lists) and know what you do and don't know first.
Research skills include good Googling, knowing the best docs and books for your area, reading mailing list archives, and reading source code.
Treat confusion as a sign you are about to learn something rather than a failure.
summary.summary: The author, a programmer who writes mostly about computer systems, argues that a positive attitude alone is not enough to learn hard things and describes specific learning skills they have practiced. The post is a personal essay rather than a formal tutorial. It walks through four skills (identifying what you don't understand, having confidence in your knowledge, asking questions, and doing research) with examples from learning Rust references and TCP ports. It also covers recognizing confusion as a signal to learn and lists skills the author still wants to improve.
